sub: Technology block (c): asynchronous communication between the systems that must never wait for each other

title: Why Message Queues?
desc: A system for asynchronous communication between applications

items: Asynchronous communication: the sender does not wait for the receiver
In the Java world specified by JMS (Java Message Service), part of Java/Jakarta EE
Supports loose coupling, scalability and reliability
Decoupling — sender and receiver work independently; a UTM service can restart without losing telemetry
Load distribution — messages are processed in parallel by many consumers
Reliability — persistent storage of messages until they are consumed
Scalability — add consumers dynamically as traffic grows

title: JMS Architecture: Queues & Topics
desc: Two delivery models cover almost every messaging need

body.code:
Point-to-Point (Queue)              Publish-Subscribe (Topic)

Producer                             Publisher
   |                                     |
   v                                     v
[ QUEUE ] --> exactly one            [ TOPIC ] --> every subscriber
              consumer gets              |    \
              each message           Subscriber A  Subscriber B

clearance requests,                  position broadcasts,
work distribution                    airspace status updates

items: Message producer — sends messages to a queue or topic; message consumer — receives them
Message queue — waiting line for messages (point-to-point model)
Topic — broadcast model for multiple receivers (publish-subscribe)
Message types: Text, Bytes, Object, Map, Stream

title: Telemetry Through a Topic
desc: The backbone of the Module 3 reference system, in three annotations

body.code: // producer — the drone gateway publishes each position fix jmsTemplate.convertAndSend("telemetry.topic", new Fix(droneId, lat, lon, alt)); // consumer A — the live map (Module 14) @JmsListener(destination = "telemetry.topic", containerFactory = "topicFactory") void onFix(Fix fix) { mapService.update(fix); } // consumer B — conflict detection, same messages, independently @JmsListener(destination = "telemetry.topic", containerFactory = "topicFactory") void detect(Fix fix) { conflictEngine.feed(fix); }

items: The gateway doesn't know or care who listens — add a flight logger next week without touching it
The map can crash and restart — conflict detection keeps running; that isolation is the whole point
Queue vs. topic is one word in the destination config — same annotation, different delivery semantics

title: Kafka: A Log, Not a Queue
desc: Same word "message" — a fundamentally different storage model

body.code:
Classic broker (ActiveMQ / RabbitMQ)     Kafka (distributed log)

Producer --> [ queue ] --> Consumer      Producer --> [ p0 | p1 | p2 ]  append-only
              consumed message                            ^
              is GONE — broker            Consumer reads at its own OFFSET
              tracks delivery              — and can REWIND and replay

smart broker, simple clients             simple broker, smart clients

body.card: What the log model buys you
items: Queues delete on acknowledge; Kafka retains messages (by time or size) — consumers just move an offset
Replay is the killer feature for telemetry: re-run yesterday's traffic through a new conflict detector — exactly what validation in Module 13 needs
Consumer groups give queue semantics on a log; a partition key of droneId gives per-drone ordering
The price: cluster operations — for a single lab service, a classic broker is the right size

rows: The classic choice for JMS in Java projects
Supports JMS via plugins; very flexible routing
Distributed log (not JMS, but similar use cases)
Massively scalable streaming — the natural fit for high-volume telemetry

items: Asynchronous messaging buys decoupling, buffering and fan-out — the sender never waits, the system never loses a message to a restart
Queue = work distribution (each message to exactly one consumer); topic = broadcast (every subscriber sees everything)
Pick the broker by guarantees, not fashion: throughput, ordering, persistence, replay
Telemetry fan-out is a topic — map, logger and conflict detection subscribe independently
Clearance processing is a queue — exactly one handler must act on each request
Incident replay wants Kafka — rewind the offset and re-fly yesterday's airspace against new logic
